items.followUp: Name the starting elements of the halogen and noble-gas groups.

rubric.why: Identifies the element at the start of the lanthanide series.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming cerium or giving its symbol or atomic number.

rubric.why: Identifies the element at the start of the actinide series.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming thorium or giving its symbol or atomic number.

modelAnswer: The lanthanide series starts from cerium (Ce).
The actinide series starts from thorium (Th).

items.followUp: Why does atomic radius generally increase down a group?

rubric.why: More occupied inner shells are present farther down a group.
rubric.description: The number of electron shells increases down the group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that extra shells are added.

rubric.why: Inner electrons shield valence electrons from the nucleus, weakening the nuclear attraction they experience.
rubric.description: The additional inner electrons increase shielding of the outer electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking increased inner-electron shielding with reduced nuclear attraction on the outer electrons.

modelAnswer: Down a group, the number of electron shells increases.
The additional inner-shell electrons increase shielding, reducing the nucleus’s attraction for the outer electrons.

items.followUp: Why is the third ionization energy greater than the second ionization energy?

accept: one electron has already been removed
rubric.why: After the first ionization, the species is a positively charged ion.
rubric.description: Removal of the first electron leaves a positive ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the positively charged ion formed after the first electron is removed.

rubric.why: The remaining electrons experience stronger attraction to the nucleus, so further ionization requires more energy.
rubric.description: The second electron is more difficult to remove and requires more energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the stronger attraction to the greater second ionization energy.

modelAnswer: After the first electron is removed, the atom becomes a positively charged ion.
The remaining electrons are attracted more strongly to the nucleus, so more energy is needed to remove the second electron.

rubric.why: A single covalent bond involves one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.description: Specifies that one pair of electrons is shared.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one pair (two) of electrons is shared.

rubric.why: The defining feature of a covalent bond is sharing between atoms.
rubric.description: States that the shared pair links two atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the pair is shared between two atoms.

modelAnswer: A single covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one pair of electrons.

items.followUp: What is the difference between a single bond and a double bond?

rubric.why: A lone pair belongs to one atom and is not used to form a bond.
rubric.description: Defines a lone pair as an unshared pair of electrons on an atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a lone pair as unshared or nonbonding and associated with one atom.

rubric.why: A bond pair is the shared pair that holds atoms together in a covalent bond.
rubric.description: Defines a bond pair as a shared pair of electrons between atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a bond pair as shared between atoms or as forming a bond.

modelAnswer: A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons on one atom that is not shared in bonding.
A bond pair is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms to form a covalent bond.

items.followUp: Why are gases easily compressed compared with solids?

rubric.why: Gas particles are separated by large spaces.
rubric.description: States that gas particles are far apart.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for referring to the large spaces between gas particles.

accept: small mass in a large volume
rubric.why: The large spaces mean little matter is present in a given volume, producing low density.
rubric.description: Connects the particle spacing with low density.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the large spaces result in low mass per unit volume.

modelAnswer: Gas particles are very far apart, with large spaces between them.
Therefore, a given volume contains little matter and gases have low density.

items.followUp: Define the transition temperature of sulfur.

rubric.why: Transition temperature describes a change between allotropic forms of an element.
rubric.description: Identifies the change as one between allotropic forms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for specifying that the forms are allotropes or naming the rhombic and monoclinic forms of sulfur.

rubric.why: The transition temperature is the temperature at which one form changes into another.
rubric.description: Defines the temperature of the allotropic change.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is the temperature at which one allotropic form changes into another.

modelAnswer: Transition temperature is the temperature at which one allotropic form of an element changes into another.

items.followUp: How can you distinguish between pure water and salt solution by evaporation?

rubric.why: A pure liquid evaporates without leaving dissolved material behind.
rubric.description: States what happens to a pure liquid on evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that the pure liquid evaporates without residue.

rubric.why: When the solvent evaporates, a non-volatile dissolved solute remains.
rubric.description: States what happens to a solution on evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that the solution leaves its dissolved solute behind.

modelAnswer: Evaporate a sample of the liquid.
A pure liquid evaporates without leaving residue, whereas a solution leaves its dissolved solute behind.
Alternatively, a pure liquid boils at a fixed temperature, while a solution generally boils over a range of temperatures.
